textbookText: i. Acoelomate: Some animals like sponges, coelenterates, and platyhelminthes donot have coelom and hence they are called acoelomate animals. ii. Pseudocoelomate: Coelom derived from blastocoel of the embryonic stage is called pseudocoelom. This type of coelom is enclosed by ectoderm and endoderm. Animals in Aschehelminthes only are acoelomate. iii. Eucoelomate or coelomate: This is the true coelom which is enclosed by mesodermal cells from both sides. It is of following types: a. Schizocoel: Coelom formed by splitting of mesoderm layer in the embryonic stage. It is found in annelida, arthropoda, mollusca and higher chordate. b. Enterocoel: In ehinoderms and hemichordate, mesodermal pouches develop from larval archenteron and then fuse to form coelom. It is called enterocoel. Example: Echinoderms and protochordates. c. Haemocoel: It is the modified form of coelom in arthropods, mollusca and some annelids in which coelom is greatly reduced and filled with blood.

5. Segmentation: Segmentation is the division of body of an animal into linear series of similar parts or sections. i. Unsegmented body: Animals such as sponges, coelenterates, nemathelminthes, mollusca, echinoderms have no segmentation of their body. ii. Metameric segmentation: It is the division of body in specific pattern, into many linear series or segments where all segments are interdependent, work together and of same stage of maturation. Example: annelida, arthropoda and chordata. iii. Psedosegmentation: Body with many independent and false segments where growth of body takes place by a type of budding or strobilization and all segments are not in the same stage of maturation. Example: tapeworms

Do you know? Diploblastic: Body is developed from two germ layer in the embryonic stage; ectoderm and endoderm. Example: Porifera and coelenterata. Triploblastic: Body is developed from three germ layer in the embryonic stage; ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. Example: All animals except sponges and coelenterates. Anterior end: Front or head end of an animal. Posterior end: Rear or tail end of an animal. Dorsal surface: Body surface facing towards the sky. Ventral surface: Body surface that faces towards the earth. Lateral side: Either sides of an organism, away from central axis. Dorso-lateral side: Towards the dorsal surface and sides of the body Ventro-lateral side: Towards the ventral surface and sides of the body Mid-dorsal side: Middle region of dorsal surface. Mid-ventral side: Middle region of ventral surface. Freshwater organism: Organisms living in river pond lakes pools (less salty water). Marine organism: Organism that lives in sea water (salty water). Amphibious animal: Animal which lives in land and water both. Solitary animal: Animal that lives alone. Colonial animal: Animal that lives in group or colony where work is divided among the members. Gregarious animal: Animal that lives in groups independently. Sedentary: Animal is normally fixed to the substratum. Sea anemone Free swimming: Animal that swims freely in water. Pelagic: Animal residing in upper surface of water. Benthic: Animal living in bottom of water sources. Lentic: Standing water such as ponds, lakes etc. Lotic: Running water such as river, stream etc. Warm-blooded (homeothermic): Body temperature remains constant. Cold-blooded (Poikilothermic): Body temperature changes according to the surrounding. Flagellum: A hair like structure arising from cell body. It is present in bacteria, euglena etc. Cilia: Minute hair like cytoplasmic processes. locomotory organs of Paramecium Pseudopodia: Locomotory organ of Amoeba Setae: Locomotory organ of Earthworm.
